function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “what‑to‑do” guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **NOTE** – The helper functions you listed are geared toward Python projects, so I’m not using them here.  
> Instead, I’m writing the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow manually – which is the usual way to handle a Node.js repo.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine is small and fast
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install only production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (check package.json or app.js)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and contains the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – adjust if your code uses a different port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory called `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and add a single file `deployment.yaml` that contains both the Deployment and Service definitions:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # will be overridden by the CI build tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Two replicas of the pod are created.  
> * The Service exposes the app on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo "${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}" | docker login -u "${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}" --password-stdin
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # (Optional) Deploy to Kubernetes – requires a KUBECONFIG secret
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v2
      #   with:
      #     manifests: |
      #       ./k8s/deployment.yaml
      #     images: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
      #     kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username.  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – the password or token.  
> * (Optional) `KUBECONFIG` – if you want the workflow to deploy automatically.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Dockerfile** in the repo root.  
* A `k8s/deployment.yaml` file containing both Deployment & Service.  
* A `.github/workflows/ci.yml` file that builds the image on every push to `main`.  
* The GitHub Actions tab should show a successful run (once the secrets are set).

That’s it! 🎉 If you run into any errors (e.g., the app uses a different port), just tweak the Dockerfile and Kubernetes YAML accordingly.
